Indigo Skate Camp

By: Nicola De Chaud | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A skate camp in the middle of nowhere...

Summary:
Pro skateboarder Dallas Oberholzer took time out from the international skate scene and set up an unusual skate camp in the Valley of a Thousand hills. Rural youth are skating their way out of the Valley and holding their own as fearless skaters both locally and internationally...

Script:


Indigo



Dallas: When you first come down the ramp you feel your heart racing it’s exiting you don’t have to sell the sport to anybody... Any children here who might be looking for something else and thinking how can they grow wings to do something beyond the valley. Thats why we came up with Indigo skate camp, let skateboarding take you places.

I made my life playing on a skate board, don’t you wanna try it out, it might take you places.

In 2002 SA skate champ, Dallas Oberholzer took time out from the international skate scene and headed for the hills of Kwazulu Natal

Dallas: Arriving her in a taxi, I mean at that point years ago I had nothing to loose. Arriving with a couple of skateboards and showing them movements. It was excitement amongst the youth

Dallas enlisted the help of an ender in the community, Mkhosi Msomi and together they began to build the indigo vision

Khosi: He lived in our house as one of our family

Dallas; So Khosi was quite an angel, she was very accommodating and welcoming she let me into her home. Cooked for me, gave me a hut. I would work on her land and then I would with a vision of finally having my land

Khosi: He had a plan but we didn’t really understand it all at first
. Until we saw the wood for the skate park

Dallas: Beautiful thing in the culture here is the sense of community. They all assisted, they saw someone was working and they shared in the experience and laughed while they did it.

Khosi: I had no problem. I was very happy for my kids to have skateboarding.
It’s like a second home to keep them off the streets and out of trouble.

Dallas: First thing I see when I see the youth is this self esteem and this sense of of pride. The look at the facility that they have built.

Gee: it’s an epic place. It’s a skate camp like in the middle of nowhere. it’s something unbelievable and every time when I’m on my board I just feel so free, it’s wehre I find my happiness. I own it by riding it.

Gee Ngubani turned up at the park 10 years ago. Over the years he developed into a class skater and a stand out leader


Dallas: Gee always had this sense of wanting to be someone and skateboarding is the perfect vehicle for him to discover his potential.
G now runs the project, which caters to 50/60 local youngsters. They run a structured programme every weekday afternoon

Dallas: So Gee would be operations manager, overseeing volunteers and taking the programme. He’s a great role model and a success story

Gee: We offer them different skills like, art skills, music and dance.

Dallas: Also to develop industry related activities like filming and photography, things that are needed in the skateboarding board

Gee: Each and every day when I come here I check on ‘how you doing, what do you think about the project, are you gaining something from us?”

Dallas: With Gee we would have never hit 5th gear. it definitely grew beyond my expectations. I simply believed that having something to do would empower them.

The children of indigo skate park are skating their way out of the valley of a thousand hills

Dallas: We have some of the best ramp skaters in the country. And they are way up there and they are blowing minds right now, they have this fearlessness and they are going just as high as can go in this country. They’ve got famous.

Gee: What we say in our slogan is you should let skateboarding take you places. It has already taken me places

Indigo kids have travelled europe to take part in international skate competitions as well as visiting every top skate event in South Africa.

It’s up to them, it’s in their hands. Everyone has a chance of getting out of this ramp and flying in the air. It’s just a matter of them putting their time in. And the more they realise it’s in their hands they more they become empowered to become anything they can become
